data.title: Behind every meme, a worry: What India's youth are really losing sleep over
data.description:
India is one of the world’s youngest countries, and its youth are growing up in unsteady times: Prices keep climbing, jobs feel less certain, and AI is reshaping work. Globally, 54 per cent of lower earners think AI will leave them behind, against 31 per cent of high earners. Scroll through their feeds and you’ll find reels and memes about all of it. But behind every meme is an actual worry. Red Lab’s new Worry Report, built from seven major surveys across more than 100 countries, including Deloitte’s Gen Z and Millennial Survey for India, tries to name them. They turn out to be ordinary: rent, health, jobs, bills, parents, the planet.
 
The money squeeze
 
For Indian youth, the anxiety starts with money. About 20 per cent of Gen Z and 19 per cent of millennials name the cost of living as a top concern. On harder measures, India fares better than the world: 20 per cent of Gen Z and 13 per cent of millennials struggle to pay monthly expenses, against 34 per cent globally for both. Financial insecurity tells the same story, at 29 per cent and 18 per cent for Gen Z and millennials, respectively, in India, versus 45 per cent and 44 per cent worldwide. 
 
The pressure shows up in decisions, not just balances. While 37 per cent of Gen Z and 20 per cent of millennials say they can’t afford a home (51 per cent and 40 per cent globally), 76 per cent of Gen Z and 62 per cent of millennials say housing costs shape their career choices. The question is no longer just which job pays well, but which city’s rent they can survive. Meanwhile, 54 per cent of Gen Z and 44 per cent of millennials have delayed a major life decision because of money.
 
Getting in, holding on 
 
Gen Z and millennials aren’t losing sleep over the same things. Gen Z is worried about getting in. Unemployment is its top concern at 27 per cent (22 per cent for millennials), and long hours are its biggest work stressor at 53 per cent. Millennials are worried about holding on — 50 per cent don’t feel supported by their leader, their top work stressor, and 45 per cent say there aren’t enough hours to finish their work.
 
The planet and the power bill
 
Climate weighs on millennials most. It is the top concern for 34 per cent of India’s millennials, against 23 per cent of Gen Z, and adds a lot of stress for 38 per cent of millennials. Yet the share naming the environment as a top-three life worry has slipped to 23 per cent from 26 per cent in September 2025.
 
Part of the reason may be the electricity bill. Worldwide, 74 per cent worry about rising energy prices. Half would put low prices first even if emissions rise. That isn’t indifference to the planet; people simply dread an unexpectedly high bill.
 
A world on edge
 
Global politics also weighs heavily on their minds. Worldwide, 69 per cent say the world got worse over the past year, a measure of pessimism rather than a sense of personal danger. Stopping wars is the top priority in 21 of the 34 countries surveyed, and among the top two in 33. Yet people haven’t given up on one another: 57 per cent want their country to cooperate on global problems even if it means compromise, up from 55 per cent in 2025, and about eight in ten would back that more if it delivered visible results. Confidence in the big powers is thin, with only 39 per cent comfortable with the US in a leading global role and 37 per cent with China.
 
Who to believe
 
Worldwide, 65 per cent believe foreign actors deliberately fill their media with falsehoods to inflame divisions, up from 54 per cent in 2021. In India, the figure is 70 per cent.
 
The people at the dinner table
 
Indian youth worry about others as much as about themselves. Globally, 48 per cent name health as a top-three worry, rising from 40 per cent among Gen Z to 59 per cent among boomers. In India, though, family health is Gen Z’s biggest stressor at 44 per cent (37 per cent for millennials).
 
Worried, not broken 
 
The data isn’t all bleak, though: 76 per cent of Gen Z and 83 per cent of millennials in India rate their mental well-being as good or extremely good, though 24 per cent of Gen Z and 18 per cent of millennials feel stressed all or most of the time. A further 73 per cent and 81 per cent say their employer takes mental health seriously, up from 70 per cent and 78 per cent in 2025.
 
What stands out is how modest the ask is. Indian youth aren’t demanding a revolution. They want rent they can manage, a job that lasts, a bill that doesn’t spike and a future they can plan around. In short, stability.

data.title: Beyond hospital beds: Bajaj bets on a new model of healthcare delivery
data.description:
At a time when India's leading hospital chains are expanding bed capacity and seeking higher revenue per occupied bed, the Bajaj Group is attempting to build a healthcare business with a different set of economics — one that relies less on hospitalisation and more on managing a patient's health over a lifetime.
 
Its healthcare venture, Bajaj Integrated Health System (BIHS), which unveiled its brand Nivara on Thursday, expects a substantial portion of its earnings to come from outside hospitals. All its doctors, including super-specialists, will be on its payroll without revenue-linked targets, while a proposed subscription-based managed care model seeks to align the interests of insurers, healthcare providers and patients.
 
 
“We believe that we are deriving profit from the lifetime value of that patient, or actually, the community,” Nirav Bajaj, managing director and chief executive officer of BIHS, told Business Standard. “Our intent is to keep you healthy and not benefit from when you are ailing,” he said.
 
The century-old conglomerate is committing ₹2,000-2,500 crore to its first integrated healthcare network in Pune, funded entirely from within the group, and aims to be present in more than 10 cities over the next 15 years. BIHS is a wholly owned subsidiary of Jamnalal Sons Pvt Ltd, an unlisted Bajaj family holding company.
 
The group's healthcare investment is pegged at ₹6,000-7,000 crore over four to five years. Bajaj did not disclose an overall investment outlay for the national expansion.
 
Even the sequencing of investments reflects a departure from the conventional hospital-centric approach. BIHS will first establish a network of medical centres, home healthcare services and ambulatory centres — facilities offering day-care surgeries, chemotherapy, dialysis and advanced diagnostics without requiring overnight hospitalisation — before commissioning its 500-bed hospital.
 
“The hospital feeds the medical centres and the ambulatory centres, not the other way around,” Bajaj said.
 
BIHS plans to establish six to nine multispecialty medical centres, at least two day surgery centres, a hospital and home healthcare services across Pune, eventually employing around 2,000 people, including doctors, nurses and allied healthcare professionals.
 
Nivara's first medical centre, spread across 12,000 sq ft at Pune's Amanora township, will open next week with more than 20 in-house specialists, followed by a second centre in a couple of months. At least two day surgery centres are expected to become operational next year. 
Construction of the hospital is expected to begin in 2027. BIHS acquired a five-acre plot within Pune Municipal Corporation limits around four months ago. By the time the hospital becomes operational, the company expects to have an established patient base and a network offering primary and specialist consultations, diagnostics, pharmacy, physiotherapy, home healthcare and day-care procedures.
 
BIHS expects to expand into multiple cities simultaneously after 2030, once it has established its Pune network. Bajaj said the company would evaluate both metros and non-metros based on their healthcare needs.
 
Acquisitions, too, are not ruled out, although the immediate priority is to establish BIHS's institutional culture across its different healthcare formats before integrating another organisation.
 
Changing the economics of healthcare
 
The commercial viability of the model will depend on BIHS's ability to generate sufficient earnings from services outside hospitals, where the nature and frequency of patient engagement would be different from those in a conventional hospital business. While the 500-bed hospital will account for a sizeable share of earnings, Bajaj expects the facilities outside it to make a substantial contribution. He declined to quantify the earnings mix, saying the company was still working with projections.
 
BIHS has set aggressive internal break-even targets, Bajaj said, without disclosing the timelines. He acknowledged, however, that the business could take somewhat longer to break even than conventional healthcare ventures, given the novelty of its model. While each facility will have its own unit economics, the company will assess profitability at an integrated healthcare system level.
 
“We build businesses for decades, not for a couple of years,” he said.
 
The model also departs from conventional practices in the way doctors are employed and incentivised. All doctors will be on the company's payroll, with their performance assessed on clinical outcomes, quality of care, patient experience and readmission rates, rather than revenue generation and patient conversion ratios. Consultations at Nivara will last a minimum of 10-12 minutes.
 
BIHS is also looking to reduce dependence on individual doctors by incorporating standardised treatment protocols and clinical pathways into its electronic medical records system. Its technology architecture comprises more than 80 applications connecting doctors, diagnostic laboratories, medical centres and patients. A single patient ID will allow medical records to be accessed across its network nationally.
 
Each patient will have a dedicated care team comprising a general physician, a nurse coach or nutritionist, and an emotional well-being coach or therapist, with specialists involved when required. The company also plans to offer allopathy, Ayurveda and homeopathy within its healthcare network.
 
Over the past few years, Bajaj and his team have studied around 35 healthcare institutions across North America, Europe and Asia. The advantage of entering healthcare through a greenfield venture, he said, was the ability to adopt global and domestic practices without the constraints of legacy systems.
 
Bringing insurers into the picture
 
A critical component of BIHS's business model will be managed care, under which patients will pay a monthly subscription for access to healthcare services, with an emphasis on preventive care, early diagnosis and continuous health management.
 
Initially, the subscription will cover outpatient services, including consultations, treatment of routine illnesses, health check-ups and specialist consultations. As its network expands, BIHS plans to extend the offering to cover the entire healthcare journey, including surgeries, under a monthly payment structure.
 
In India, where health insurance coverage remains largely centred on hospitalisation, financing outpatient and preventive care will be critical to the success of such a model.
 
Having insurance companies within the Bajaj Group gives BIHS an opportunity to develop such products. Bajaj said the group companies would, however, deal with each other at arm's length, and BIHS would also work with external insurers.
 
“Whether it is the right way or not, time will tell. But we believe that this is the way healthcare should be delivered and experienced in India,” Bajaj said.

data.title: EPFO approves systematic withdrawal plan for retiring members savings
data.description:
The retirement fund body EPFO on Thursday approved a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for its retiring members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire corpus at once.
 Under the SWP, retiring members of the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation will receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once, a Labour Ministry release said.
 The decision was taken at the 240th meeting of the Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), chaired by Union Minister for Labour & Employment and Youth Affairs & Sports, Mansukh Mandaviya.
 
 The Board approved a proposal to introduce a Systematic Withdrawal Plan, enabling retiring EPF members to receive their accumulated provident fund savings in periodic instalments instead of withdrawing the entire amount at once.
 This reform will enable retiring members to withdraw their accumulated provident fund savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference.
 This facility would provide members with a structured source of periodic income while allowing the remaining corpus to continue generating returns, thereby helping augment their retirement income and supplement their pension benefits.
 The facility would be entirely voluntary, with no compulsion on members to opt for withdrawals.
 The option may also be extended to eligible family members/beneficiaries, ensuring greater flexibility and financial security for the family. This aims to ensure stable post-retirement income, reduce reinvestment risks, strengthen fund sustainability, and extend social security coverage to gig and platform workers.
 SWP will enable members to convert their retirement savings into a stable and predictable stream of systematic withdrawals post-retirement, while preserving ownership of the underlying corpus.
 Approximately 6.32 lakh EPF members aged above 55 years with provident fund accumulations exceeding Rs 5 lakh are expected to be the primary beneficiaries of the proposed SWP framework during the initial phase.

data.title: Rupee extends gains for fourth straight session on strong foreign inflows
data.description:
The Indian rupee appreciated for the fourth consecutive session on Thursday, supported by strong foreign portfolio inflows into domestic equities and a revival in overseas investment in government bonds. The domestic currency settled at 93.30 per US dollar, compared with its previous close of 93.45.
 
The rupee gained ground despite a relatively strong dollar, with softer crude oil prices and the return of foreign capital providing support. However, the strength of the greenback remains a key risk for the domestic currency. The dollar index, which measures the US currency against a basket of six major currencies, was down 0.1 per cent at 103.7 on Thursday after touching a high of 103.8. The index remained elevated following signals from the US Federal Reserve that further interest rate increases could be considered.
 
 
Minutes of the October meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) showed that almost all officials felt further rate hikes could be appropriate. Some members also indicated that an increase of more than 25 basis points (bps) could be considered in December. Fed Governor Christopher Waller also floated the possibility of a 50 bps hike.
 
Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) bought more than ₹88,000 crore worth of Indian equities in November so far, marking the highest monthly pace of inflows since November 2020. During the November 2020 buying phase, the Nifty rallied 12 per cent over three months and 30 per cent over 12 months.
 
The return of foreign investor interest is also extending to the debt market, which has witnessed a turnaround in inflows. After three consecutive months of net selling, overseas investors bought $1.1 billion worth of Indian government bonds in November.
 
The yield differential between Indian and US 10-year government bonds widened to 2.20 percentage points as of November 16 from 1.94 percentage points in September, improving the relative returns on Indian bonds for overseas investors. Foreign holdings of index-linked government securities also rose to nearly two-month highs.
 
ICICI Securities said the rupee broke out of its six-month consolidation range of 96.85-94.15, signalling a potential trend reversal.
 
"This bodes well for further appreciation in the rupee towards an implied target of the 91 per dollar mark eventually," the brokerage said in a report.
 
"Technically, the rupee has immediate support around 93.10-93.30, followed by 93.00. On the upside, 94.90-95.20 remains the next important resistance zone," said Amit Pabari, managing director at CR Forex.

data.title: Subhash Chandra case: NCLT gives CBI, parties 3 weeks to file responses
data.description:
The National Company Law Tribunal on Thursday directed the CBI to file its response within three weeks in the personal insolvency proceedings against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra, while asking all parties to jointly prepare a common compilation of documents.
 A five-member special bench of the tribunal, headed by its President Justice Anupinder Singh Grewal, also granted three weeks to the parties, including the resolution professional (RP), to file a single convenience compilation containing all documents they intend to rely upon during the proceedings.
 "The CBI shall file its response within three weeks. The parties can also file the convenience compilation within three weeks," the bench said.
 
 The bench also asked the CBI to file its response directly before the tribunal and ensure that its counsel appears in the proceedings.
 The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has directed that the matter be listed on December 9 for the next hearing.
 Earlier, during the last hearing on September 23, the NCLT issued notice to the probe agency CBI in the personal insolvency matter of Subhash Chandra and said the interim director restraining Essel Group Chairman from alienating property will continue till its final decision.
 The NCLT issued notice after being informed that a creditor had filed a complaint before the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), which is conducting its enquiry.
 During the hearing, counsel appearing for the RP informed the bench that notices had been served on all respondents in compliance with its earlier directions and an affidavit of service had been filed. However, the RP would be moving an application seeking condonation of delay in filing the affidavit, as service on some parties had taken additional time.
 The bench emphasised that there would be only one common convenience compilation, and all three sides - the RP, creditors and other respondents - would have to jointly prepare it. It clarified that the RP could not file a separate compilation and that all documents sought to be relied upon by the RP must also be included in the common set.
 The CBI has registered an FIR against Subhash Chandra for allegedly inflating his net worth to avail loans from the Life Insurance Corporation Housing Finance Limited (LICHFL) and then becoming a defaulter, causing a loss of more than Rs 1,322 crore to the public-sector lender.
 LICHFL alleged in its complaint, now part of the FIR, that Chandra submitted net-worth certificates used to secure approval and disbursal of two loans totalling Rs 980 crore.
 The LICHFL was one of the lenders that had approached NCLT, opposing a recent repayment plan allowing creditors to recover only about Rs 6.5 crore from Chandra's personal estate against claims of roughly Rs 22,006 crore

data.title: Irdai to form working groups on real-time health claims tracking, metrics
data.description:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) plans to set up two industry working groups within the next 10 days to improve transparency in health claims processing and standardise performance metrics across insurers, Irdai Chairman Ajay Seth said on Thursday.
 
Speaking at the CII Financing Summit, Seth said the working groups would be formed under the Insurance Advisory Committee, following the constitution of a sub-committee. “We are in the process of forming two working groups with the industry and expect it may be in about 10 days’ time to form those industry groups,” he said.
 
One working group will examine ways to provide real-time visibility into the health insurance claims process, including pre-authorisation, hospital discharge, and claims settlement. The other will work on developing standardised performance metrics for claims and grievance redress to enable comparisons across insurers.
 
 
Questioning the industry’s reliance on claims settlement ratios, Seth said the commonly used metric, which is largely based on the number of claims decided, does not necessarily reflect policyholders’ experience. The figures could include claims that are paid in full or in part, repudiated, rejected or closed.
 
For policyholders, the more relevant measure is whether the insurer has paid the full amount claimed, rather than simply the number of claims settled, he said.
 
Irdai wants insurers to compete on product performance, claims responsiveness, and grievance redress, backed by common definitions and disclosures.
 
Seth also flagged shortcomings in the industry’s grievance redress mechanism, pointing out that around 60 per cent of grievances, when reconsidered by senior executives within insurance companies, are resolved in favour of policyholders. Similarly, around 60 per cent of the remaining cases taken up by insurance ombudsmen are also decided in favour of policyholders.
 
He said insurers should treat grievances as feedback to improve product design, sales practices, claims decisions, and customer service, rather than merely as cases to be disposed of.
 
Seth also highlighted delays in claims processing caused by repeated requests for documentation. He said insurers should communicate documentation requirements upfront to minimise subsequent queries and delays.
 
On motor insurance, he flagged the large number of pending motor accident claims before tribunals. Nearly 1 million cases are pending, against which insurers have created reserves of around ₹87,000 crore. Some cases date back several decades, with the oldest cited by him dating to 1989.
 
Seth also said Irdai was examining the Ayushman Bharat Health Account as a common identity framework for health insurance. This could help insurers improve underwriting and offer more competitive pricing, particularly when individuals move between group and individual health insurance policies, as information on their previous coverage may not be readily available.
 
On the proposed Public Insurance Registry, Seth said the initiative was intended to improve transparency around insurance products, insurers’ market conduct, and distributors. He clarified that the focus was on data governance rather than creating a centralised database, with minimal centralisation of information.
 
He also called for customers to be able to access product information and pricing without having to share personal details upfront. “The product is needed for the general public. It is a regulated product, but personal details are being sought before a price is given. That is not how an industry should build itself, particularly when it is talking about expanding coverage,” he said, describing the requirement as a “toll” on consumers.
 
Seth said insurance products should be accessible for comparison before customers are asked to provide personal information. He also called for plain-language summaries in local languages explaining policy coverage, exclusions, and returns.
 
The proposed measures, he said, were aimed at strengthening trust in the insurance sector, with the policyholder’s experience at the time of a claim being the ultimate test of the promise made when a policy is sold.

data.title: Paytm to invest up to ₹200 crore in Singapore, buy 19.1% in CardUp
data.description:
Paytm parent One 97 Communications on Thursday said its Singapore arm will invest up to Rs 200 crore in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Societies, including about Rs 162 crore for a 19.1 per cent stake in its payments subsidiary CardUp.
 The board of Paytm Singapore Pte Ltd, a step-down wholly owned subsidiary of One 97 Communications, approved a partnership with Funding Asia Group Pte Ltd (Funding Societies) at a meeting on Thursday, the company said in a regulatory filing.
 The initial investment of about Rs 162 crore, or up to SGD 21.8 million, will be made in cash for the issuance of shares in CardUp Pte Ltd, a payments subsidiary of Funding Societies. The remaining investment of about Rs 38 crore may be made in one of Funding Societies' affiliates, it said.
 
 Paytm expects the CardUp transaction to be completed by May 20, 2027.
 One 97 Communications will also enter into a business and technology partnership with CardUp, under which it will provide payments and lending technology to the Singapore firm to expand Paytm's technology-led payments and financial services stack in Singapore.
 The company will receive technology fees and a revenue share under the agreement, which will be initially valid for five years with a right of renewal on mutually acceptable terms, the filing said.
 The move is in line with the company's previously disclosed roadmap to expand its presence in select international markets through a "partner operated" model, under which it provides its acceptance platform and devices while the local partner leads sales, distribution and on-ground operations to serve merchants, the company said.
 It said it will monetise its contributions through licensing fees, revenue sharing and other arrangements while deploying limited capital.
 CardUp, incorporated in Singapore in 2015, is in the digital payments business. Its turnover rose to Rs 299.20 crore in calendar year 2025 from Rs 194.38 crore in 2024 and Rs 104.16 crore in 2023.
 Funding Societies, a small and medium enterprises (SME) digital financing platform, acquired CardUp for an undisclosed amount in 2024.
 In a separate disclosure in the same filing, One 97 Communications said it has completed an additional investment of Rs 500 crore in its wholly owned subsidiary Paytm Cloud Technologies Ltd, which in turn invested Rs 500 crore in Paytm Singapore.

data.title: PFRDA weighs higher distributor commissions, changes to pension fund mix
data.description:
The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) Chairman, S Ramann, said on Thursday that the regulator was examining ways to increase distributor commissions and make pension products more attractive as payouts to distributors remain significantly lower than those in the mutual fund industry.
 
He was addressing the Gatekeepers of Governance 2026 event in Mumbai.
 
Despite increasing the pool of commissions available to distributors by 2.5 times, payouts in the pension sector were still around a fifth of the levels offered by mutual funds, Ramann said. The low commissions have been one reason pension products have not gained wider acceptance, he added.
 
 
The regulator was also assessing the cost of distributor commissions for subscribers over the long term, given that pension investments could remain in place for 30 to 50 years. The impact of commissions needed to be assessed over the entire investment period, including their compounding effect, while balancing distributor incentives against the overall cost to subscribers.
 
“We actually have a bit of an inverse problem as compared to the insurance industry where money on the table for the distributors is so abysmally low that it is one of the reasons why probably the pension product never really went out in a big way. So, even after having increased the total sort of distributable commissions that lie on the table two and a half times, we’re still one-fifth the commission’s level which is available in the mutual fund industry,” he said.
 
Alongside distribution, PFRDA was reviewing the investment allocation of pension funds to improve long-term returns, including the scope for higher exposure to growth assets and alternative investment funds (AIFs).
 
The regulator has set up two expert committees to examine asset allocation: one headed by former State Bank of India Chairman Dinesh Khara and the other by investment expert Narayan Ramachandran, who has experience in the mutual fund industry. The committees have provided inputs on whether pension savings are invested in suitable asset classes to generate better returns for retirement payouts.
 
Ramann pointed to Australia’s superannuation system, where 72 per cent of the pension corpus remains invested in growth assets and the remaining 28 per cent in fixed-income instruments. Nearly half of the allocation to growth assets remains in unlisted investments.
 
India’s pension system remains risk-averse, with relatively little capital flowing into greenfield projects and startups. To widen investment opportunities, the National Pension System (NPS) has started its own fund of funds to invest in AIFs, allowing pension savings to participate in a diversified pool of investments.
 
PFRDA is also examining the possibility of introducing a market-based guarantee mechanism for pension payouts to private-sector subscribers. A committee headed by Sahu is studying the proposal, though such guarantees would involve an additional cost for subscribers.
 
Ramann said the regulator would examine the proposal and consider introducing changes gradually.

data.title: Mis-selling starts with sales targets, not branch counters: RBI DG Murmu
data.description:
Mis-selling of financial products often stems from sales targets and variable pay structures rather than actions at the branch level, said S C Murmu, deputy governor (Dy Guv) of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). He urged financial institutions to examine whether their incentive structures reward sales volumes or customer outcomes, and how these are measured.
 
“Look hard at incentives. Mis-selling rarely begins at the branch counter. It begins with a sales target and a variable pay scheme. Ask what your incentives actually reward: volumes or customer outcomes. And ask how you measure each,” Murmu said, speaking at an event in Mumbai.
  
Mis-selling has remained a concern across India's financial sector, particularly in the distribution of insurance policies, and mutual fund (MF) and other third-party products through banks and financial institutions.
 
Murmu also highlighted the significant regulatory changes awaiting banks from April 1, 2027, when the new prudential framework is scheduled to come into effect. The transition will involve the introduction of expected credit loss (ECL)-based provisioning, implementation of the remaining Basel III standards, and adoption of a new standardised approach to credit risk.
 
Under the ECL framework, banks will have to make provisions for losses they expect to incur rather than only for losses that have already materialised. The framework will replace the existing incurred-loss-based provisioning approach.
 
Under the new norms, banks will classify financial assets into three stages based on changes in credit risk, and make provisions accordingly. Stage 1 assets will attract provisions for 12-month expected credit losses, while assets in Stages 2 and 3 will require provisions based on lifetime expected credit losses.
 
The changes will make the banking system more sensitive to risk and place greater responsibility on boards, Murmu said.
 
With the shift towards principle-based regulation, boards will have greater flexibility in determining their institutions' risk appetite. However, this will also increase their responsibility to define that appetite in both qualitative and quantitative terms, and hold the management accountable for adhering to it.
 
Murmu also highlighted the importance of investments in technology and people, saying these were no longer optional for financial institutions. Boards needed to understand how technology was being deployed and the risks associated with it.
 
He also pointed to changes in the RBI's governance directions for banks, which came into effect on October 1, 2026. The revised directions replaced checklist-based board agendas with principle-based guidance, doing away with a long list of prescribed routine agenda items. This would free up board time, which directors should use to focus more on strategy and risks, including technology-related risks, and ensure preparedness for the transition to the new prudential framework in April 2027, he said.
 
Murmu called for closer coordination among financial sector regulators, given the overlap in their mandates. A listed bank, for instance, is subject to the RBI's prudential norms and related-party lending guidelines, as well as the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (Sebi’s) listing regulations governing related-party transactions.
 
He further said that cyber resilience requires common baseline standards, as a single incident could affect a bank, an insurer, and a market infrastructure institution simultaneously.
 
“Regulation does not keep pace by writing rules faster. It keeps pace by being clearer about what it expects of those who run and oversee institutions, and then by trusting their judgement,” he said.

data.title: Delhi HC says restaurants, hotels cannot impose mandatory service charges
data.description:
The Delhi High Court on Thursday clarified that it had not granted any interim protection to restaurants and hotels against an earlier order prohibiting them from automatically collecting service charges from customers.
 
A Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma said no interim relief had been granted against the single judge's March 28, 2025, order.
 
The clarification came after Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, appearing for the Centre, pointed out that some restaurants continued to treat service charges as compulsory despite the High Court's earlier ruling.
 
Sharma submitted that the practice was contrary to the single judge's order, which upheld the Central Consumer Protection Authority's (CCPA) 2022 guidelines prohibiting hotels and restaurants from adding service charges to bills by default.
 
 
"Ball is in your court. It is for you to take action. We can't take action. Where is the interim relief? Where is the interim relief in their favour? We have not granted any interim prayer," Acting Chief Justice Sambre observed.
 
The Bench was hearing appeals filed by the National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI) and the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations of India (FHRAI) challenging the single judge's decision. The court admitted the appeals for hearing.
 
The CCPA issued its guidelines in July 2022 after receiving complaints from consumers about restaurants adding service charges, typically ranging between 5 and 20 per cent, to food bills without their consent.
 
The NRAI and FHRAI challenged the guidelines, contending that service charges were a longstanding industry practice and were linked to employee compensation and labour arrangements.
 
However, the single judge found no material to establish that the charges directly benefited employees. The court held that payment of service charges must remain voluntary and that compelling customers to pay them amounted to an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
 
The ruling also upheld the CCPA's authority to regulate such practices and held that its guidelines were legally binding.
 
The single judge further restrained restaurants from using the term 'service charge' in a manner that could mislead consumers into believing it was a government-imposed levy. Establishments were asked to use alternative descriptions such as 'voluntary contribution' or 'staff welfare fund'.
 
Restaurants were also directed not to add such charges automatically to bills and to clearly inform customers that tipping was optional.
 
In its appeal, the NRAI has argued that service charges should not be treated as an unfair trade practice when their collection is disclosed on menus and at restaurant premises.
 
It has also contended that the practice is recognised in the hospitality industry and forms part of employee compensation under labour arrangements.
 
The association has questioned whether the dispute should be examined under labour law rather than consumer protection law. It has further challenged the CCPA's authority to regulate pricing structures that customers are informed of and accept while placing orders.
